Appendix B Scoring update relative to the published version of the original audit

While re-running the benchmark we revised two steps of the original scoring and one style index. The revised arXiv version of the original audit [33] uses the same code. Table 12 lists the numbers that change relative to the published version, and Figure 5 shows the change in the ranking. Here every sample is scored on the same 100 respondents. For this reason some values differ from the revised version of the original audit in the third decimal. The in-sample copula differs more, because that paper scores it on all 263 draws (PSS 0.936).

Reverse-keyed items.

Human answers to the 13 reverse-keyed items are stored reversed, so that a high value always means a positive attitude. Model answers to these items were stored as given to the original wording and were not reversed before scoring. We now reverse them with x′=min+max−xx^{\prime}=\min+\max-x and call the result the aligned score. The published scores are raw. A consistent respondent with a positive attitude therefore scored high on a reverse-keyed item in the human file and low in the model file. Item DUN_02 (“I usually resist new ideas”) shows the size of the effect. The human mean is 4.14 after reversal, while gpt-5.4-mini answers 1.97 on average, which is close to the human mean before reversal (1.86). The change raises the PSS of every one of the 36 C3 cells of the original audit, by a median of 0.093 and at least 0.016. For gpt-5.4-mini the aligned PSS is 0.743. The change affects all five components. It removes divergence on 13 items, restores the sign of their correlations with the other 55 items, changes the Dunham α\alpha, and enters the attitude composites used for mediation and demographic contrasts. Table 14 shows that the raw comparison roughly doubles the divergence on reverse-keyed items. Our raw recomputation of gpt-5.4-mini gives 0.703, against the published 0.714. The gap comes from pooling. For most models the published version averaged the 20 test-retest repeats into the C3 cell, while we use the single run of the main grid for every model. We also checked whether the gain of each model follows its keying gap. The rank correlation is 0.21 (p=0.23p{=}0.23), so the gain depends on more than this one property.

Baseline totals.

The distribution component was missing from the totals of the statistical baselines and counted as zero. With it included, the copula of the original audit reaches 0.927 on the same 100 IDs. This copula is fit on the 263 people it is scored against, so we also report an out-of-sample copula, fit on the 163 people outside the headline sample, which reaches 0.824. The analysis script computes item distances for every cell and selects the rows of one cell by matching model, condition, presentation mode and reasoning effort. Baseline samples have no reasoning-effort value, and a missing value never matches itself. The selection was empty, and the total treated the missing component as zero. The published copula total of 0.688 is the weighted sum of the other four components alone.

Acquiescence.

The index of the original audit, the forward-item mean minus the reverse-item mean, grows with answers that follow the content of the items. We keep it under the name keying gap and add the balanced acquiescence index (ARS) [6]. The keying gap gives zero to a respondent who agrees with every statement and a large positive value to a respondent who follows the content of the items. ARS is the average of the forward-item mean and the reverse-item mean on a 0–1 scale, minus 0.5, computed on raw answers. With ARS computed in this way for humans and models, gpt-5.4-mini shifts by +0.21 human SD. Humans have a larger keying gap (2.001) than gpt-5.4-mini (1.512). Applying the keying gap to reversed human answers and unreversed model answers reproduces the published shift for gpt-5.4-mini (+1.28 against the published +1.29).

Ranking.

The first change raises some models more than others, so the order of the LLMs changes (Figure 5). The Spearman correlation between the published and the revised order is 0.79. gpt-5.4-mini moves from first to 10th place, and MiniMax M3 (0.813), MiniMax M2.7 (0.809) and Kimi K2.7 Code (0.802) now lead. The correlation component gains most and rises for every cell (median +0.37). The reliability component also rises for every cell (median +0.11), because the unreversed items had moved the Dunham α\alpha of some models far from the human value. The mediation component falls for 30 of 36 cells (median −-0.18). The order changes mainly through the reliability and mediation components, whose changes differ most between models (SD 0.18 and 0.19, against 0.07 for correlation).

What holds and what changes.

The main conclusion of the original audit holds and becomes stronger. LLM samples are not a drop-in replacement for human data, and the lead of the statistical baseline grows. In its published version the best LLM was slightly above the copula. With the revised scoring the in-sample copula is above every language model, by +0.11 [+0.06, +0.17] over the best one (Table 2), and the out-of-sample copula is level with the best (+0.01 [−-0.07, +0.09]). Range restriction holds as well, because it does not depend on item direction. The share of extreme answers is 0.270 for humans and 0.024 for gpt-5.4-mini. LLM samples still produce mediation paths that humans do not show (Section 5.11). The revision changes three findings. First, the best LLM is a different model. Second, the acquiescence finding becomes a pattern of fewer extreme answers, more midpoint answers and a smaller keying gap. Third, the advantage of LLMs on mediation and demographic effects shrinks, as the next paragraph shows.

Mediation and demographic effects.

The original audit argued that these components are where language models add value over statistical baselines. Against the in-sample copula this does not hold. Its mediation component is 0.968 against 0.929 for gpt-5.4-mini, and its demographic component is 0.663 against 0.489 (Table 1). Against the out-of-sample copula the mediation component is 0.722, and the paired difference to gpt-5.4-mini is −-0.21 [−-0.39, −-0.03]. Its demographic component is 0.382, with a difference of −-0.11 [−-0.35, +0.13], which is within noise. Neither copula sees the profile, so its demographic component reflects chance agreement only, and the gap between the two copulas shows how noisy this component is at n=100n{=}100. PSS scores only one indirect effect, and gpt-5.4-mini reproduces it better than the real answers of the same 100 people do (mediation component 0.929 against 0.707). The same sample produces 6 of the 7 cross-construct mediation paths that are absent in the human data.

Analyses not affected.

Results that compare models only with each other, such as inter-LLM similarity and test-retest reliability, do not depend on the direction of reverse-keyed items. The revised version of the original audit recomputes the analyses that compare models with humans through these items. It also signs the paired differences of its counterfactual swaps by the direction of the swap and reports the swap effects in units of the human SD. Without the sign, swaps in opposite directions cancel, which made the role effect look small.

Appendix C Models, costs and item keying

Table 13 lists the decision models with their pinned versions, context limits, prices and the cost of the C3 grid. Table 14 compares the item divergence of reverse-keyed and forward-keyed items under the raw and the aligned scoring.

Appendix D All generative cells

Table 15 lists the PSS components of all 47 generative cells under the revised scoring, with the raw PSS for the cells of the original audit.

Appendix E Reference sample

Table 16 scores the main sources against the full reference of 263 people and against the 100 headline people alone. Section 5.1 discusses it.

Appendix F Agreement between models and sensitivity to the weights

The published version of the original audit found that LLMs agree with each other more than with humans. On the correlation structure, decision models agree with each other (0.384) slightly less than with humans (0.422, Figure 6). Their errors thus show little shared bias on this measure.

The ranking of decision models and baselines is stable under changes of the PSS weights. Over 500 Dirichlet draws the mean Spearman correlation with the canonical ranking is 0.95 (minimum 0.71; 0.60 of draws above 0.95). The in-sample copula is first in every draw. Independent marginals, Tev1 4B and Solar Decide Flash form the bottom three in a share of 0.48 of the draws. The changes happen inside the close middle group.

Appendix G Reproducibility

All scripts are in scripts/psychometry/. run_decision_c3.py sends the decision requests and stores one JSON file per respondent and model with the full probability vectors, the resolved model version, the token count and the cost. It skips cells that are already complete, so an interrupted run can be resumed. 01_generate_synthetic.py is the generator of the original audit; the new generative models were run with --model-set update_2026_10_models --conditions C3_full --reasoning-effort minimal. score_decision_c3.py computes raw and aligned PSS and recomputes gpt-5.4-mini from the data of the original audit as a check. analyze_decision_c3.py runs the readout, response-style, predictive-validity, null-mediation, probability and similarity analyses. analyze_generative_c3.py rescores every generative cell with both scoring paths and computes its style and downstream measures. bootstrap_decision_c3.py adds the oracle and the out-of-sample copula and runs the paired bootstrap over all sources. run_decision_controls.py sends the C0, retest and swap grids, and analyze_decision_controls.py analyses them. analyze_decision_forecasts.py scores the probability vectors, the references and the generative repeat distributions as forecasts. analyze_decision_references.py reads the profile regression as a synthetic respondent and runs the checks against the 100 headline people. analyze_decision_structure.py computes the correlation level, the eigenvalue shares, the subscale separation and Tucker’s φ\varphi. make_decision_paper_assets.py builds every table, figure and number in this paper from the resulting CSV files. No API call is needed after the generation scripts.
